questions.question: What is gRPC and what does it stand for?

options.text: Google Remote Procedure Call - a high-performance RPC framework

questions.explanation: gRPC is Google's open-source RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers. It enables efficient, strongly-typed communication between services, popular in microservices architectures.

questions.question: What serialization format does gRPC use by default?
questions.explanation: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers—a binary serialization format that's smaller and faster than JSON/XML. Schemas are defined in .proto files and compiled to generate client/server code.

questions.question: Which gRPC communication patterns are supported? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Server streaming (single request, stream of responses)
Client streaming (stream of requests, single response)

questions.explanation: gRPC supports all four patterns: unary (like REST), server streaming (e.g., live feeds), client streaming (e.g., file upload), and bidirectional streaming (e.g., chat). This flexibility exceeds REST's request-response model.

questions.question: Why is gRPC generally faster than REST with JSON?

options.text: Binary protobuf is smaller and faster to serialize than text-based JSON

questions.explanation: Protocol Buffers are binary (smaller payloads), have schema-based serialization (faster parsing), and gRPC uses HTTP/2 (multiplexing, header compression). Combined, these provide significant performance gains.

questions.question: What is a .proto file in gRPC?

options.text: A schema definition file that defines services and message types

questions.explanation: .proto files define the API contract: message types (like structs), services (like interfaces), and RPC methods. The protoc compiler generates client and server code in multiple languages from this schema.

questions.question: A team is building a public API for third-party developers. Should they use gRPC or REST?

options.text: REST is typically better for public APIs due to wider tooling support and browser compatibility

questions.explanation: REST is more accessible for public APIs: works in browsers, curl, any HTTP client. gRPC requires specific client libraries and doesn't work directly in browsers. gRPC excels for internal service-to-service communication.

questions.question: How does gRPC handle backward compatibility when schemas change?

options.text: Field numbers in protobuf enable adding/deprecating fields without breaking clients
Version numbers in URLs like REST

questions.explanation: Protobuf uses field numbers, not names, for serialization. New fields get new numbers; old clients ignore unknown fields. Removing fields (by number) is safe if old numbers aren't reused. This enables gradual evolution.

questions.question: What HTTP version does gRPC require?
questions.explanation: gRPC requires HTTP/2 for multiplexing (multiple requests over one connection), bidirectional streaming, and header compression. This is why gRPC doesn't work directly in browsers (limited HTTP/2 support).

questions.question: True or False: gRPC can only be used between services written in the same programming language.
questions.explanation: gRPC is language-agnostic. The .proto schema compiles to client/server code in many languages (Go, Java, Python, C++, etc.). A Go service can communicate with a Python service seamlessly.

questions.question: What is gRPC-Web and why does it exist?

options.text: A web framework built on gRPC
A protocol that enables browsers to communicate with gRPC services via a proxy

questions.explanation: Browsers can't make native gRPC calls (HTTP/2 limitations). gRPC-Web is a protocol where browsers make HTTP/1.1 requests to a proxy (like Envoy) that translates to gRPC for backend services.

questions.question: Which scenarios are ideal for gRPC? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Microservices communication within a data center

questions.explanation: gRPC excels at internal service communication, streaming, and high-performance scenarios. Public mobile APIs can use gRPC but REST is often simpler. Browser-based public APIs typically use REST or GraphQL.

questions.question: How does gRPC handle errors compared to REST?

options.text: gRPC uses HTTP status codes like REST
gRPC has its own status codes (OK, CANCELLED, INVALID_ARGUMENT, etc.)

questions.explanation: gRPC defines its own status codes (16 codes like OK, NOT_FOUND, INTERNAL) that map to but differ from HTTP codes. This provides consistent error semantics across languages and transports.
